key_insight: LLM scientific claim verifiers can reach different verdicts depending on how they interpret an underspecified claim, so the interpretation should be recorded alongside the answer.
engineering_relevance: For AI research agents and benchmark systems, exposing the agent’s claim interpretation improves traceability, makes disagreements diagnosable, and helps compare verdicts more fairly.
method: Defined a 9-field “Claim Card” to capture a verifier’s interpretation before evidence gathering, with fields marked stated, inferred, or default.
Ran a GPT-5.4 agent 5 times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims under three conditions: with a card, without a card, and with a frozen card.
Deliberately edited one card field (quantifier or support threshold) to test how interpretation changes affect verdicts and downstream tool use.
evidence_signal: Across 900 runs, more than 40% of card fields were not stated; adding a card cost about 10% more tokens/time but did not measurably change agreement with expert labels, while targeted card edits changed verdicts on about one-third of claims (p < 0.001).
watch_item: A recorded interpretation may still be incomplete or inconsistently constructed, so benchmarks need a standard way to publish and compare both the claim label and the underlying interpretation.
paper_title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
